subject: Mathematics

syllabus: VCE Mathematics Study Design (from 2023), General Mathematics Units 1 and 2

units.title: Unit 1: Data, sequences and finance, linear relations and matrices

points.title: Types of data
points.brief: Categorical data sorts into groups (nominal or ordinal). Numerical data is counted (discrete) or measured (continuous).

points.title: Displaying categorical data
points.brief: Frequency tables, bar charts and segmented bar charts show how often each category occurs.

points.title: Histograms, stem plots and dot plots
points.brief: Displays for numerical data, chosen to suit the data and the question, that show shape, centre, spread and outliers.

points.title: Mean, median and mode
points.brief: The mean is the sum divided by the count, the median the middle value and the mode the most common. Skew pulls the mean toward the tail.

points.title: Range, IQR and standard deviation
points.brief: The range is highest less lowest, the IQR is Q3 less Q1, and the standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.

points.title: The five-number summary and boxplots
points.brief: Minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum, drawn as a boxplot. Values beyond the fences, 1.5 IQRs past the quartiles, are possible outliers.

points.title: Shapes of distributions
points.brief: Distributions can be symmetric or skewed, and in a bell-shaped one most data lie within a few standard deviations of the mean.

points.title: Comparing distributions
points.brief: Back-to-back stem plots and parallel boxplots compare the centre and spread of one variable across two or more groups.

points.title: Arithmetic sequences
points.brief: Each term adds the same common difference, d. The nth term is a + (n − 1)d.

points.title: Geometric sequences
points.brief: Each term is multiplied by the same common ratio, r. The nth term is a × r^(n − 1).

points.title: First-order recurrence relations
points.brief: A rule giving each term from the one before, such as u(n+1) = u(n) + 4, with a starting value u0.

points.title: Explicit rules for sequences
points.brief: A rule for the nth term, such as t = a + (n - 1)d, finds any term without listing every one before it.

points.title: Linear growth and decay
points.brief: Adding or subtracting the same amount each step, as in simple interest or flat-rate depreciation.

points.title: Geometric growth and decay
points.brief: Multiplying by the same factor each step, as in compound interest or reducing balance depreciation.

points.title: Percentage increase and decrease
points.brief: Working out percentage increases and decreases, mark-ups and discounts.

points.title: GST and price
points.brief: GST in Australia is 10%. A price including GST is the price without it times 1.1.

points.title: The unitary method
points.brief: Finding the value of one unit first, such as 1 per cent or one item, then scaling up to compare and solve problems.

points.title: Simple interest
points.brief: Interest on the starting amount only, I = PrT/100, so the balance grows by the same amount each period.

points.title: Compound interest
points.brief: Interest added to the balance and earning interest itself, A = P(1 + r/100)^n with r per period.

points.title: Comparing purchase options
points.brief: Comparing paying cash, by debit or credit card, with a personal loan, or with buy now pay later, by total cost.

points.title: Inflation and purchasing power
points.brief: Inflation means the same money buys less over time, so a price rising with inflation stays the same in real terms.

points.title: Gradient and intercept
points.brief: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (rise over run) and c is the y-intercept.

points.title: Finding a linear rule
points.brief: Two points give the gradient, then substituting one point gives the intercept.

points.title: Linear models in context
points.brief: A gradient is a rate, such as cost per kilometre, and the intercept is a starting value, such as a call-out fee.

points.title: Simultaneous linear equations
points.brief: The intersection of two lines solves both equations, found by graphing, substitution or elimination, such as a break-even point.

points.title: Piecewise and step graphs
points.brief: Graphs made of line segments or steps model situations such as tax scales, phone charges and parking fees.

points.title: What a matrix is
points.brief: A rectangular array of rows and columns that stores information such as a database or the links in a network. Types include row, column, square, zero and identity.

points.title: Adding and scaling matrices
points.brief: Matrices of the same order add element by element. Scalar multiplication multiplies every element.

points.title: Multiplying matrices
points.brief: An m × n matrix times an n × p matrix gives an m × p matrix, each element a row times a column.

points.title: Identity and inverse matrices
points.brief: The identity matrix leaves a matrix unchanged. A square matrix with a non-zero determinant has an inverse.

points.title: Matrices in context
points.brief: Matrices can store data such as sales by shop and month, and multiplying them can total costs or revenue.

points.title: Transition matrices
points.brief: A matrix of the chances of moving between states, multiplied again and again to show how a population changes and settles.

units.title: Unit 2: Associations, networks, variation and measurement

points.title: Response and explanatory variables
points.brief: The explanatory variable may explain or predict changes in the response variable, and goes on the horizontal axis.

points.title: Scatterplots
points.brief: A scatterplot shows the link between two numerical variables, with the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis.

points.title: Describing an association
points.brief: An association is described by its direction, form and strength. A strong association does not prove that one variable causes the other.

points.title: Lines of good fit
points.brief: A line drawn through a scatterplot by eye can be used to predict one variable from the other.

points.title: Interpolation and extrapolation
points.brief: Predicting within the data's range is interpolation and is more reliable than extrapolation beyond it.

points.title: Vertices, edges and degree
points.brief: A graph has vertices joined by edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges that meet it.

points.title: Types of graphs and the adjacency matrix
points.brief: Graphs can be connected, isomorphic, or have loops and multiple edges. An adjacency matrix records which vertices are joined.

points.title: Planar graphs and Euler's formula
points.brief: A planar graph can be drawn without edges crossing, and then v − e + f = 2.

points.title: Walks, trails, paths and circuits
points.brief: A walk is any route, a trail repeats no edge, a path repeats no vertex, and a circuit or cycle ends where it began.

points.title: Shortest path
points.brief: In a weighted graph, the shortest path between two vertices has the smallest total weight.

points.title: Trees and minimum spanning trees
points.brief: A tree connects all vertices with no cycles. A minimum spanning tree does so with the least total weight, found by a greedy algorithm.

points.title: Direct and inverse variation
points.brief: In direct variation y = kx; in inverse variation y = k/x. Each can be recognised from a table, a graph or a rule.

points.title: Transforming data to linearity
points.brief: Plotting y against x squared, 1/x or log x can turn a curved pattern into a straight line.

points.title: Modelling non-linear data
points.brief: Rules of the form y = kx^n fit some curved data, and the transformed straight line gives k.

points.title: Units and precision
points.brief: Units of length, angle, area, volume and capacity, exact and approximate answers, scientific notation and significant figures.

points.title: Perimeter and area
points.brief: Perimeter and area of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, arcs, sectors and composite shapes.

points.title: Surface area and volume
points.brief: Volume of a prism is base area times height. Surface area adds the areas of every face.

points.title: Similarity and scale factors
points.brief: Similar shapes have equal angles and sides in the same ratio. Conditions for similarity show when two triangles are similar.

points.title: Scaling area and volume
points.brief: If lengths scale by k, areas scale by k squared and volumes by k cubed.

points.title: Pythagoras' theorem
points.brief: In a right-angled triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other sides, in two and three dimensions.

points.title: Sine, cosine and tangent ratios
points.brief: The trigonometric ratios find sides and angles in right-angled triangles, including angles of elevation and depression.

points.title: The sine and cosine rules
points.brief: The sine rule, with its ambiguous case, and the cosine rule solve triangles without a right angle.

points.title: Area of a triangle with sine
points.brief: Area = ½ab sin C, using two sides and the angle between them.

points.title: Three-figure bearings
points.brief: Directions measured clockwise from north, such as 135°T, used with the sine and cosine rules in navigation problems.
